0201: \end{center}
0202: 
0203: The algebraic-solution rationality step is also prior.  Ostrowski treats the
0204: linear multiplicative equation
0205: \(\Phi(\varphi(z))=g(z)\Phi(z)\) for rational data
0206: \cite{Ostrowski1968AlgebraicSolutions}; that equation does not directly cover
0207: the square in \(F(z^2)=H(z)^{-1}F(z)^2\).  Kumiko Nishioka's
0208: Theorem~5.1.7 is the standard reference for the rational--transcendental
0209: dichotomy for \(k\)-Mahler functions defined by a linear functional equation
0210: \cite[Theorem~5.1.7]{Nishioka1996MahlerFunctions}; see also the modern
0211: restatement and proof in \cite[Corollary~8]{BellCoonsRowland2013MahlerDichotomy}.
0212: Our equation is quadratic in \(F\) and therefore outside that linear class;
0213: Keiji Nishioka's nonlinear class \(f(z^p)=\mathscr R(z,f(z))\) is the
0214: applicable result.  The one-variable specialization of his 1985 theorem says
0215: that if
0216: \(f(z^p)=\mathscr R(z,f(z))\), with \(\mathscr R\) rational and \(f\)
0217: algebraic over \(\CC(z)\), then \(f\in\CC(z)\)
0218: \cite{Nishioka1985AlgebraicSolutions}.  Taking
0219: \(p=2\) and \(\mathscr R(z,Y)=Y^2/H(z)\) proves the rationality used in
0220: \Cref{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}; that rationality is not claimed as a
0221: contribution of this paper.
0222: 
0223: The nearest algorithms compute rational solutions of linear Mahler equations
0224: \cite{ChyzakDreyfusDumasMezzarobba2018MahlerSolutions} and first-order
0225: factors through Riccati equations whose monomials are products of successive
0226: shifts of the unknown
0227: \cite{ChyzakDreyfusDumasMezzarobba2025FirstOrderFactors}.  The present equation
0228: \(P_0(z)R(z)^2=P_1(z)R(z^2)\) repeats the unshifted unknown; a rational
0229: monomial substitution preserves that repeated exponent and does not turn it
0230: into a product of distinct successive shifts.  We therefore do not claim the
0231: first decision procedure for general Mahler--Riccati problems or a lower
0232: complexity than those algorithms.  The effective addition here is the
0233: input-only \(O(D\log D)\) degree bound, an explicit height bound, and a single
0234: finite Pad\'e reconstruction for this normalized multiplicative equation.
0235: Additive Mahler summability \cite{ArrecheZhang2022MahlerResidues} concerns a
0236: different equation.
0237: 
0238: Accordingly, the claimed contributions are limited to three linked steps:
0239: parity-compatible algebraic collision lifting (with Kumiko Nishioka's
0240: special-value theorem and Keiji Nishioka's algebraic-solution rationality
0241: theorem cited for their respective steps), effective rational-coboundary bounds and
0242: reconstruction, and cross-base finite radial determination for elementary
0243: two-groups.  The class Euler products, their character expansion, the general
0244: periodic-data dictionary, Keiji Nishioka's algebraic-to-rational theorem, and the
0245: analytic identity-theorem recovery statement are background rather than
0246: novelty claims.  Boyle--Schmieding's computable periodic invariants
0247: \cite{BoyleSchmieding2017FiniteGroupExtensions} and represented
0248: cospectrality and switching in gain-graph theory
0249: \cite{Zaslavsky1989BiasedGraphs,CavaleriDAngeliDonno2021BalanceGainGraphs,
0250: CavaleriDonno2022Cospectrality} delimit the dynamical side further.
0251: 
0252: Three printed open-problem interfaces delimit the claim.  Boyle and
0253: Schmieding ask to ``characterize the polynomials \(\det(I-tA)\) arising from
0254: \(G\)-primitive matrices'' and to ``characterize the trace series \(T_A\) and
0255: conjugate trace series \(\kappa T_A\)''
0256: \cite[Realization Problems~6.1(2)--(3)]{BoyleSchmieding2017FiniteGroupExtensions}.
0257: Our theorem starts with two realized extensions, so its determinant and trace
0258: formulas do not solve either positivity-realization problem.  Chyzak,
0259: Dreyfus, Dumas, and Mezzarobba leave open polynomial-time solution of general
0260: linear Mahler equations for all order--degree regimes
0261: \cite[Sec.~4.3]{ChyzakDreyfusDumasMezzarobba2018MahlerSolutions}; our finite
0262: Pad\'e criterion treats one normalized nonlinear coboundary equation and does
0263: not settle that complexity problem.  O'Hare asks for finite-data rigidity for
0264: unimodal and Markov maps \cite[Introduction]{OHare2025FiniteDataRigidity}.
0265: The present theorem is an exact symbolic result for orbit-class Euler data,
0266: not a derivative-data rigidity theorem for those maps.
0267: 
0268: The separately submitted Supplementary Material contains the Frobenius-class Mertens correction from which the profiles arose, its
0269: quotient-cover refinement, and the exact \(S_3\) witness are now separated
0270: from the inverse argument.  This paper uses only
0271: the fixed-label coordinate and does not claim that the underlying Mertens
0272: product or Frobenius equidistribution is new.
0273: 
0274: \subsection{Organization}
0275: 
0276: Section~\ref{sec:framework} establishes the represented determinant and
0277: Adams--M\"obius formulas.  Section~\ref{sec:boundary-collisions} contains the
0278: collision, lifting, effective coboundary, finite-sampling, and general radial
0279: recovery theorems.  Section~\ref{sec:exactness} records the verification
0280: boundary.  The appendices give the radial continuation convention and the
0281: standard periodic-data dictionary.

 succeeded in 317ms:
0001: \begin{theorem}[Effective normalized rational coboundary criterion]
0002: \label{thm:effective-rational-mahler-coboundary}
0003: Let \(P_0,P_1\in\ZZ[z]\) be coprime, with
0004: \(P_0(0)=P_1(0)=1\).  Put \(d_i=\deg P_i\) and \(D=d_0+d_1\).
0005: If \(D=0\), then \(P_0=P_1=1\), and the unique normalized solution is
0006: \(R=1\).  If \(D>0\), put
0007: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-bounds}
0008:  L=\lfloor\log_2D\rfloor,
0009:  \qquad
0010:  N=b_2(D)=D\lceil\log_2(2D)\rceil,
0011: \end{equation}
0012: and
0013: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-height-bound}
0014:  \Lambda=h(P_0)+h(P_1)
0015:    +\frac12\log\bigl((d_0+1)(d_1+1)\bigr),
0016:  \qquad
0017:  K=N\log2+D(L+1)\Lambda.
0018: \end{equation}
0019: There is a finite algorithm over \(\QQ\), using only \(P_0,P_1\), which
0020: decides whether
0021: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-equation}
0022:  \frac{P_0(z)}{P_1(z)}
0023:  =\frac{R(z^2)}{R(z)^2},
0024:  \qquad R\in\QQ(z)^\times,\quad R(0)=1,
0025: \end{equation}
0026: and constructs \(R\) when it exists.  The solution is unique.  In its unique
0027: reduced form
0028: \[
0029:  R=\frac{A}{B},
0030:  \qquad A,B\in\ZZ[z],\quad (A,B)=1,\quad A(0)=B(0)=1,
0031: \]
0032: it satisfies
0033: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-output-bounds}
0034:  \deg A+\deg B\le N,
0035:  \qquad
0036:  \max\{h(A),h(B)\}\le K.
0037: \end{equation}
0038:  In particular, \(\max\{\deg A,\deg B\}\le
0039:  D\lceil\log_2(2D)\rceil\).  Two necessary conditions
0040: are
0041: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-obstructions}
0042:  d_0=d_1,
0043:  \qquad P_0\equiv P_1\pmod2.
0044: \end{equation}
0045: 
0046: More explicitly, let \(S(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}s_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) be the
0047: unique formal solution of
0048: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-formal-equation}
0049:  P_0(z)S(z)^2=P_1(z)S(z^2).
0050: \end{equation}
0051: Writing \(p_{i,j}=[z^j]P_i\), its coefficients are obtained successively from
0052: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-coefficient-recurrence}
0053: \begin{split}
0054:  2s_n={}&
0055:  \sum_{\substack{0\le j\le d_1\\j\le n,\ n-j\ {\rm even}}}
0056:    p_{1,j}s_{(n-j)/2} \\
0057:  &-\sum_{\substack{0\le j\le d_0,\ u,v\ge0,\ u+v=n-j\\
0058:           (j,u,v)\ne(0,0,n),(0,n,0)}}p_{0,j}s_us_v
0059:  \qquad(n\ge1).
0060: \end{split}
0061: \end{equation}
0062: After computing \(s_0,\ldots,s_{2N}\), solve the affine linear system
0063: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-pade-system}
0064:  \sum_{j=0}^N b_js_{k-j}=0
0065:  \quad(N+1\le k\le2N),
0066:  \qquad b_0=1,\qquad s_m=0\ (m<0).
0067: \end{equation}
0068: If it is inconsistent, reject.  Otherwise choose any solution, put
0069: \[
0070:  B_*(z)=\sum_{j=0}^Nb_jz^j,
0071:  \qquad
0072:  A_*(z)=\sum_{k=0}^N
0073:        \left(\sum_{j=0}^{\min\{k,N\}}b_js_{k-j}\right)z^k,
0074: \]
0075: cancel their common factor, and normalize both constant terms to one.  Accept
0076: the resulting \(A/B\) precisely when
0077: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-final-identity}
0078:  P_0(z)A(z)^2B(z^2)=P_1(z)A(z^2)B(z)^2.
0079: \end{equation}
0080: Thus the procedure requires neither factorization over
0081: \(\overline{\QQ}\) nor enumeration of divisors.
0082: \end{theorem}
0083: 
0084: \begin{proof}
0085: Suppose first that \(R\) exists.  The degree estimate is
0086: \Cref{prop:logarithmic-mahler-divisor-bound} with \(p=2\).  For the height
0087: estimate, retain the following support information.  For
0088: \(\alpha\in\overline{\QQ}^{\times}\), set
0089: \[
0090:  r(\alpha)=\operatorname{ord}_{z=\alpha}R,
0091:  \qquad
0092:  e(\alpha)=\operatorname{ord}_{z=\alpha}(P_0/P_1).
0093: \]
0094: The map \(z\mapsto z^2\) is unramified at \(\alpha\ne0\), so
0095: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-divisor-recurrence}
0096:  e(\alpha)=r(\alpha^2)-2r(\alpha).
0097: \end{equation}
0098: Along the forward square orbit, write \(r_j=r(\alpha^{2^j})\) and
0099: \(e_j=e(\alpha^{2^j})\).  Iteration gives
0100: \[
0101:  r_0=2^{-m}r_m-\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}2^{-j-1}e_j.
0102: \]
0103: The divisor of \(R\) has finite support, so \(r_m\) is bounded.  Letting
0104: \(m\to\infty\), and using \(\abs{e_j}\le D\), gives
0105:     \(\abs{r(\alpha)}\le D\).  If \(r(\alpha)\ne0\), the forward orbit must
0106: meet the support of \(e\).  If \(k\) is its first such index, then
0107: \(r_{j+1}=2r_j\) for \(j<k\); hence
0108: \[
0109:  2^k\le2^k\abs{r_0}=\abs{r_k}\le D,
0110:  \qquad k\le L.
0111: \]
0112: Consequently every finite non-zero zero or pole of \(R\) is a zero of
0113: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-window-polynomial}
0114:  W(z):=\prod_{k=0}^{L}P_0(z^{2^k})P_1(z^{2^k}).
0115: \end{equation}
0116: Because each input polynomial is primitive and has constant term one, every
0117: rational irreducible factor of \(W\), normalized to have constant term one,
0118: lies in \(\ZZ[z]\).  The multiplicity bound above therefore gives
0119: \[
0120:  A(z)B(z)\mid W(z)^D\quad\hbox{in }\ZZ[z].
0121: \]
0122:  This divisibility will be used only for the height estimate; the sharper degree
0123:  bound has already been obtained from
0124:  \Cref{prop:logarithmic-mahler-divisor-bound}.
0125: 
0126: Let \(M(\,\cdot\,)\) denote Mahler measure.  The standard estimates
0127: \[
0128:  \log M(Q)\le h(Q)+\frac12\log(\deg Q+1),
0129:  \qquad
0130:  h(Q)\le\deg Q\log2+\log M(Q)
0131: \]
0132: and \(M(Q(z^m))=M(Q)\) give
0133: \[
0134:  \log M(W)\le(L+1)\Lambda.
0135: \]
0136: Mahler measure is multiplicative, and a non-zero integral polynomial has
0137: measure at least one.  The preceding divisibility thus implies
0138: \[
0139:  \log M(A),\ \log M(B)\le D(L+1)\Lambda.
0140: \]
0141: Together with the degree bound, this proves
0142: \eqref{eq:effective-mahler-height-bound}--
0143: \eqref{eq:effective-mahler-output-bounds}.
0144: 
0145: At infinity,
0146: \(\operatorname{ord}_\infty R(z^2)=2\operatorname{ord}_\infty R\), so the right-hand side
0147: of \eqref{eq:effective-mahler-equation} has order zero there.  This proves
0148: \(d_0=d_1\).  Moreover, reduction modulo two gives
0149: \(A(z^2)=A(z)^2\) and \(B(z^2)=B(z)^2\).  Hence the right-hand side is one
0150: in \(\mathbb F_2(z)\), proving \(P_0\equiv P_1\pmod2\).
0151: 
0152: The two occurrences of \(s_n\) on the left of
0153: \eqref{eq:effective-mahler-formal-equation} have coefficient two; every
0154: other coefficient in degree \(n\) involves only
0155: \(s_0,\ldots,s_{n-1}\).  This proves
0156: \eqref{eq:effective-mahler-coefficient-recurrence} and the uniqueness of
0157: \(S\).  If a rational solution exists, its Taylor series is \(S\).  The
0158: degree bound therefore implies that its denominator occurs among the
0159: solutions of \eqref{eq:effective-mahler-pade-system}.
0160: 
0161: It remains to justify that an arbitrary solution of that system is harmless.
0162: For two resulting pairs \((A_i,B_i)\), one has
0163: \[
0164:  B_iS-A_i=O(z^{2N+1}),
0165: \]
0166: and consequently
0167: \[
0168:  A_1B_2-A_2B_1=O(z^{2N+1}).
0169: \]
0170: The polynomial on the left has degree at most \(2N\), and hence vanishes
0171: identically.  Thus every solution of the affine system produces the same
0172: rational approximant.  If a genuine \(R\) exists, this approximant is \(R\);
0173: conversely, \eqref{eq:effective-mahler-final-identity} is exactly the cleared
0174: form of \eqref{eq:effective-mahler-equation}.  The final identity therefore
0175: gives both sound rejection and complete reconstruction.  Uniqueness also
0176: follows from the normalized injectivity of \(\delta\) proved in
0177: \Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate}.
0178: \end{proof}
0179: 
0180: \begin{remark}[Termination and a conservative bit bound]
0181: \label{rem:effective-rational-mahler-complexity}
0182: Let
0183: \[
0184:  d=\max\{1,d_0,d_1\},
0185:  \qquad
0186:  \tau=1+\max_i\left\lceil\log_2\norm{P_i}_\infty\right\rceil,
0187:  \qquad b=\tau+\log(D+1).
0188: \]
0189: All loops stop at \(2N\), and the only linear system has \(N\) equations and
0190: \(N\) unknowns.  If the parity condition in
0191: \eqref{eq:effective-mahler-obstructions} holds, the
0192: Dieudonn\'e--Dwork argument of
0193: \Cref{lem:critical-mahler-integrality} applies verbatim to
0194: \eqref{eq:effective-mahler-formal-equation}, so \(S\in\ZZ[[z]]\).  On the
0195: circle
0196: \[
0197:  \abs z=\rho:=(4d2^\tau)^{-1}
0198: \]
0199: one has \(\abs{P_i(z)-1}\le1/4\).  The convergent local product for \(S\)
0200: is
0201: \[
0202:  S(z)=\prod_{\nu\ge0}
0203:  \left(\frac{P_1(z^{2^\nu})}{P_0(z^{2^\nu})}\right)^{2^{-\nu-1}}.
0204: \]
0205: Indeed,
0206: \[
0207:  \abs{P_i(z)-1}
0208:  \le\frac{d2^{\tau-1}\rho}{1-\rho}<\frac14,
0209: \]
0210: and the logarithm series gives
0211: \(\abs{\log S(z)}\le2\log(4/3)<\log2\).  Thus
0212: \(\abs{S(z)}<2\) on the circle, and Cauchy's estimate gives
0213: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-coefficient-size}
0214:  \abs{s_n}\le2(4d2^\tau)^n.
0215: \end{equation}
0216: Thus the required series coefficients have \(O(Nb)\) bits.  In Bareiss
0217: fraction-free elimination, every intermediate entry is a minor and has
0218: \(O(N^2b)\) bits.  With schoolbook integer arithmetic, the complete procedure
0219: therefore uses
0220: \begin{equation}\label{eq:effective-mahler-bit-complexity}
0221:  O(N^7b^2)\quad\hbox{bit operations},
0222:  \qquad O(N^4b)\quad\hbox{bits of storage}.
0223: \end{equation}
0224: These deliberately elementary bounds prove polynomial-time termination; no
0225: claim of optimality is made.  Fast integer and modular linear algebra improve
0226: them, but an exact sharper exponent would require a separate complexity
0227: analysis.
0228: \end{remark}
0229: 
0230: \begin{corollary}[Same-base effective specialization]
0231: \label{cor:same-base-effective-rational-mahler}
0232: Let \(A\) be an \(n\times n\) non-negative integral matrix and let \(B,B'\)
0233: be integral matrices satisfying
0234: \[
0235:  \abs{B_{ij}},\abs{B'_{ij}}\le A_{ij},
0236:  \qquad B_{ij}\equiv B'_{ij}\equiv A_{ij}\pmod2.
0237: \]
0238: Assume that
0239: \(P_0=\det(I-zB)\) and \(P_1=\det(I-zB')\) are coprime, and put
0240: \(a_*=\max\{1,A_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n\}\).  Then the algorithm of
0241: \Cref{thm:effective-rational-mahler-coboundary} decides and constructs every
0242: normalized rational certificate for \(P_0/P_1\), using integer coefficient
0243: recursion before the Pad\'e step.  Uniformly,
0244: \begin{equation}\label{eq:same-base-effective-input-bounds}
0245:  D\le2n,\qquad N\le2n\lceil\log_2(4n)\rceil,\qquad
0246:  h(P_0),h(P_1)\le n\log(na_*),
0247: \end{equation}
0248: and one may use
0249: \begin{equation}\label{eq:same-base-effective-height-bound}
0250:  K\le N\log2+2n(\lfloor\log_2(2n)\rfloor+1)

 succeeded in 313ms:
0201: \end{equation}
0202: Consequently, on \(|z|<\lambda^{-1}\),
0203: \begin{equation}\label{eq:artin-determinant-log}
0204:   L_{\chi_\rho}(z):=-\Log_0P_\rho(z)
0205:   =\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{T_n(\chi_\rho)}{n}z^n
0206:   =\sum_{r\geq1}\frac{\Pi_{\psi^r\chi_\rho}(z^r)}{r}.
0207: \end{equation}
0208: Here \(\Log_0P_\rho\) is the analytic germ at zero normalized by
0209: \(\Log_0P_\rho(0)=0\).
0210: \end{lemma}
0211: 
0212: \begin{proof}
0213: Expanding the block product in \(A_\rho^n\) sums \(\rho(\tau(q))\) over
0214: closed length-\(n\) paths, with a trace over \(V_\rho\); this is
0215:   \eqref{eq:twisted-trace}.  The finite-matrix identity
0216: \[
0217:   -\Log_0\det(I-zB)=\sum_{n\geq1}\Tr(B^n)z^n/n
0218: \]
0219: gives the second expression in \eqref{eq:artin-determinant-log}.  A primitive
0220: orbit \(\gamma\) of length \(d\) contributes its \(d\) cyclic base points to
0221: period \(n=rd\), and its repeated holonomy is \(g_\gamma^r\).  Division by
0222:   \(n=rd\) leaves the factor \(1/r\), proving the last expression.  Absolute
0223:   convergence follows from \Cref{lem:perron-weighted-domination} on every
0224:   smaller disc.
0225: \end{proof}
0226: 
0227: \begin{proposition}[Standard zeta interpretation in the binary case]
0228: \label{prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
0229: Let \(G=C_2\), write \(A=A_e+A_s\) for the matrices counting edges with
0230: labels \(e\) and \(s\), and put \(B=A_e-A_s\).  The adjacency matrix of the
0231: standard two-sheeted skew-product edge shift is
0232: \[
0233:  \widetilde A_\tau=
0234:  \begin{pmatrix}A_e&A_s\\ A_s&A_e\end{pmatrix}.
0235: \]
0236: Its Artin--Mazur zeta function satisfies
0237: \begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}
0238:  \zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)
0239:  =\det(I-z\widetilde A_\tau)^{-1}
0240:  =\frac{1}{\det(I-zA)\det(I-zB)}.
0241: \end{equation}
0242: Consequently, for two binary labellings \(\tau,\tau'\) on the same marked
0243: base, with sign blocks \(B,B'\),
0244: \begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
0245:  \frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}
0246:  =\frac{\zeta_{\widetilde X_{\tau'}}(z)}
0247:         {\zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)}.
0248: \end{equation}
0249: Thus the rational function used in the binary inverse theorem is a ratio of
0250: standard dynamical zeta functions, not an additional invariant.
0251: \end{proposition}
0252: 
0253: \begin{proof}
0254: The change of basis
0255: \((u,v)\mapsto(u+v,u-v)\) conjugates \(\widetilde A_\tau\) over \(\QQ\) to
0256: \(A\oplus B\).  Taking determinants gives
0257: \eqref{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}.  The common base determinant cancels
0258: for \(\tau\) and \(\tau'\), giving \eqref{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}.
0259: \end{proof}
0260: 
0261: For a general class function, write
0262: \[
0263:   \phi=\sum_{\rho\in\Irr(G)}
0264:      \widehat\phi(\rho)\chi_\rho,
0265:   \qquad
0266:   \widehat\phi(\rho)
0267:     =\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\phi(g)\overline{\chi_\rho(g)},
0268: \]
0269: and define \(L_\phi=\sum_\rho\widehat\phi(\rho)L_{\chi_\rho}\).  This agrees
0270: with the orbit expansion in \eqref{eq:artin-determinant-log}.  The Adams
0271: operation \(\psi^m\) acts on class functions by
0272: \((\psi^m\phi)(g)=\phi(g^m)\).  It need not preserve irreducibility or
0273: positivity, but it has a finite character expansion
0274: \begin{equation}\label{eq:adams-coefficients}
0275:   \psi^m\chi_\rho=\sum_{\pi\in\Irr(G)}
0276:       a_{\rho,\pi}^{(m)}\chi_\pi,
0277:   \qquad
0278:   a_{\rho,\pi}^{(m)}
0279:      =\langle\psi^m\chi_\rho,\chi_\pi\rangle_G.
0280: \end{equation}
0281: The coefficients are periodic in \(m\) modulo the exponent of \(G\), and
0282: therefore uniformly bounded.
0283: 
0284: \subsection{Adams--M\"obius primitive inversion}
0285: 
0286: Primitive Euler coordinates and periodic ghost coordinates are related by the
0287: classical necklace/Witt M\"obius transform
0288: \cite{MetropolisRota1983Necklaces}.  The point specific to the present problem
0289: is that a Frobenius-class product retains the fixed primitive label before the
0290: Adams power operation is applied.  Applying the classical transform to this
0291: fixed-label coordinate and then to the finite twisted-determinant family gives
0292: the formulas below.
0293: 
0294: \begin{theorem}[Primitive and fixed-label determinant coordinates]
0295: \label{thm:adams-mobius}
0296: For every class function \(\phi\) and \(|z|<\lambda^{-1}\),
0297: \begin{align}
0298:   \Pi_\phi(z)
0299:     &=\sum_{m\geq1}\frac{\mu(m)}{m}
0300:        L_{\psi^m\phi}(z^m),
0301:        \label{eq:primitive-adams-mobius}\\
0302:   F_\phi(z):=\sum_{r\geq1}\frac{\Pi_\phi(z^r)}{r}
0303:     &=\sum_{r,m\geq1}\frac{\mu(m)}{rm}
0304:        L_{\psi^m\phi}(z^{rm}).
0305:        \label{eq:fixed-adams-mobius}
0306: \end{align}
0307: For \(\phi=\chi_\rho\), insertion of \eqref{eq:adams-coefficients} gives a
0308: formula involving only the finite determinant family:
0309: \begin{equation}\label{eq:fixed-determinant-open-disc}
0310:   F_{\chi_\rho}(z)=
0311:   \sum_{r,m\geq1}\frac{\mu(m)}{rm}
0312:     \sum_{\pi\in\Irr(G)}a_{\rho,\pi}^{(m)}
0313:       \bigl(-\Log_0P_\pi(z^{rm})\bigr).
0314: \end{equation}
0315: All three series are absolutely convergent on compact subsets of the Perron
0316: disc after expansion into primitive orbits.
0317: \end{theorem}
0318: 
0319: \begin{proof}
0320: By \Cref{lem:trace-log},
0321: \[
0322:   L_{\psi^m\phi}(z^m)
0323:   =\sum_{\gamma\in\cP}\sum_{r\geq1}
0324:      \frac{\phi(g_\gamma^{mr})}{r}z^{mr|\gamma|}.
0325: \]
0326: Multiplying by \(\mu(m)/m\), summing, and putting \(s=mr\), the coefficient
0327: of \(\phi(g_\gamma^s)z^{s|\gamma|}\) becomes
0328: \[
0329:   \sum_{m\mid s}\frac{\mu(m)}{m(s/m)}
0330:   =\frac1s\sum_{m\mid s}\mu(m).
0331: \]
0332: It is one for \(s=1\) and zero otherwise.  This proves
0333: \eqref{eq:primitive-adams-mobius}.  Summing that identity over \(z^r/r\)
0334: proves \eqref{eq:fixed-adams-mobius}.  Finally use the character expansion
0335: \eqref{eq:adams-coefficients} and \eqref{eq:artin-determinant-log}.
0336: 
0337: For convergence, the total number \(p_n\) of primitive length-\(n\) orbits
0338: satisfies \(p_n\leq\Tr(A^n)/n\ll\lambda^n/n\).  Thus the orbit expansions
0339: are dominated on \(|z|\leq R<\lambda^{-1}\) by convergent logarithmic series.
0340: This also justifies every rearrangement above.
0341: \end{proof}
0342: 
0343: The difference between the periodic and fixed-label transforms is now
0344: formal rather than terminological.
0345: 
0346: \begin{proposition}[Exact Artin-substitution obstruction]
0347: \label{prop:artin-substitution-obstruction}
0348: On \(|z|<\lambda^{-1}\),
0349: \begin{equation}\label{eq:exact-f-minus-l}
0350:   F_\phi(z)-L_\phi(z)
0351:   =\sum_{r\geq2}\frac{
0352:        \Pi_\phi(z^r)-\Pi_{\psi^r\phi}(z^r)}{r}.
0353: \end{equation}
0354: Writing \(\Pi_\phi(z)=\sum_{n\geq1}c_n(\phi)z^n\), the two germs agree if
0355: and only if
0356: \begin{equation}\label{eq:coefficient-obstruction}
0357:   \sum_{r\mid n}\frac1r
0358:     c_{n/r}(\phi-\psi^r\phi)=0
0359:   \qquad(n\geq1).
0360: \end{equation}

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let (p\ge2), let (P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]) have constant term one, and let
+(q\ge1) be an integer for which (qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]).  The unique formal
+series (F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first (h+1) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator (d_h) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of (z^n) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the (p) factors of (F^p)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is (f_j)
+with (j<n); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where (s\ge2), all (j_i\ge1), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set (c=pq).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below (n), a linear term (f_j), (j<n), has
+denominator dividing (c^{2j-1}\), hence (c^{2n-2}).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus (c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by (c) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with (n), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Algebraic critical products are rational coboundaries]
\label{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}
Let (H\in\QQ(z)^\times), (H(0)=1), and suppose that
(F\in1+z\QQ[[z]]) is algebraic over \(\CC(z)\) and satisfies
(F(z)^2=H(z)F(z^2)).  Then (H=\delta R) for a unique
(R\in\QQ(z)^\times) with (R(0)=1).
\end{proposition}

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let (p\ge2), let (P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]) have constant term one, and let
+(q\ge1) be an integer for which (qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]).  The unique formal
+series (F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first (h+1) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator (d_h) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of (z^n) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the (p) factors of (F^p)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is (f_j)
+with (j<n); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where (s\ge2), all (j_i\ge1), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set (c=pq).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below (n), a linear term (f_j), (j<n), has
+denominator dividing (c^{2j-1}\), hence (c^{2n-2}).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus (c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by (c) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with (n), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}

0354: \begin{lemma}[Critical quadratic zero estimate]
0355: \label{lem:critical-mahler-zero-estimate}
0356: Let \(P_0,P_1\in\CC[z]\) have constant term one, set
0357: \(\eta=\max\{\deg P_0,\deg P_1\}\), and let an analytic germ
0358: \(F(0)=1\) satisfy
0359: \[
0360:  P_1(z)F(z)^2=P_0(z)F(z^2).
0361: \]
0362: If \(F\) is transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then every non-zero
0363: \(Q\in\CC[z,Y]\) with \(\deg_zQ\le D\) and \(\deg_YQ\le N\) satisfies
0364: \begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-mahler-zero-bound}
0365:  \operatorname{ord}_{z=0}Q(z,F(z))
0366:  \le D+4DN+\eta N^2.
0367: \end{equation}
0368: \end{lemma}
0369: 
0370: \begin{proof}
0371: First take an irreducible factor \(q\in\CC[z,Y]\) of positive
0372: \(Y\)-degree and write \(d=\deg_zq\), \(n=\deg_Yq\).  Clear the denominator
0373: in its pullback by setting
0374: \[
0375:  \widetilde q(z,Y)=P_0(z)^n
0376:  q\!\left(z^2,\frac{P_1(z)}{P_0(z)}Y^2\right).
0377: \]
0378: This is a polynomial, with
0379: \begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-pullback-orders}
0380:  \deg_Y\widetilde q=2n,\qquad
0381:  \deg_z\widetilde q\le2d+\eta n,\qquad
0382:  \operatorname{ord}_0\widetilde q(z,F(z))
0383:  =2\operatorname{ord}_0q(z,F(z)).
0384: \end{equation}
0385: If \(q(0,1)\ne0\), then \(\operatorname{ord}_0q(z,F(z))=0\), so there is
0386: nothing to prove.  Assume henceforth that \(q(0,1)=0\).
0387: We claim that \(q\nmid\widetilde q\).  Otherwise the irreducible curve
0388: \(C:q=0\) is invariant under the rational map
0389: \[
0390:  \Phi(z,Y)=\left(z^2,\frac{P_1(z)}{P_0(z)}Y^2\right).
0391: \]
0392: Pass to the normalization of \(C\).  The induced map permutes forward the
0393: finite set of places above \((0,1)\), so this finite dynamical system contains
0394: a periodic place.  Its Puiseux germ \(Y=G(z)\), based at \((0,1)\), therefore
0395: satisfies for some \(\ell\ge1\) the \(\ell\)-fold iterate of the same equation
0396: as \(F\).  Consequently \(U=G/F\) obeys
0397: \[
0398:  U(z^{2^\ell})=U(z)^{2^\ell},\qquad U(0)=1.
0399: \]
0400: If \(U=1+cz^\alpha+\cdots\), with \(c\ne0\) and the least positive Puiseux
0401: exponent \(\alpha\), the least non-constant exponents on the two sides are
0402: respectively \(2^\ell\alpha\) and \(\alpha\), a contradiction.  Thus
0403: \(U=1\), which would make \(F=G\) algebraic.  This proves the claim.
0404: 
0405: Hence \(R_q(z)=\operatorname{Res}_Y(q,\widetilde q)\) is non-zero.  A
0406: B\'ezout identity in \(Y\), evaluated at \(Y=F(z)\), and
0407: \eqref{eq:critical-pullback-orders} imply
0408: \[
0409:  \operatorname{ord}_0q(z,F(z))
0410:  \le\operatorname{ord}_0R_q
0411:  \le\deg R_q
0412:  \le4dn+\eta n^2.
0413: \]
0414: Finally write \(Q=a(z)\prod_iq_i^{e_i}\), separating its polynomial content
0415: in \(z\).  The content contributes at most \(D\).  With multiplicities,
0416: \(\sum_i e_id_i\le D\) and \(\sum_i e_in_i\le N\); therefore
0417: \(\sum_i e_id_in_i\le DN\) and
0418: \(\sum_i e_in_i^2\le N^2\).  Summing the factor bounds proves
0419: \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-zero-bound}.
0420: \end{proof}
0421: 
0422: Kumiko Nishioka's Theorem~5.1.7 is the standard reference for the linear
0423: Mahler rational--transcendental dichotomy: it applies to \(k\)-Mahler
0424: functions defined by a linear functional equation
0425: \cite[Theorem~5.1.7]{Nishioka1996MahlerFunctions}; see also
0426: \cite[Corollary~8]{BellCoonsRowland2013MahlerDichotomy}.  The equation
0427: \(F(z^2)=H(z)^{-1}F(z)^2\) is quadratic in \(F\) and therefore lies outside
0428: that class; Keiji Nishioka's nonlinear class
0429: \(f(z^p)=\mathscr R(z,f(z))\) is the applicable result.
0430: 
0431: \begin{proposition}[Algebraic critical products are rational coboundaries]
0432: \label{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}
0433: Let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\), \(H(0)=1\), and suppose that
0434: \(F\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) is algebraic over \(\CC(z)\) and satisfies
0435: \(F(z)^2=H(z)F(z^2)\).  Then \(H=\delta R\) for a unique
0436: \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(R(0)=1\).
0437: \end{proposition}
0438: 
0439: \begin{proof}
0440: Keiji Nishioka's algebraic-solution theorem states, in its one-variable
0441: specialization, that an algebraic Laurent-series solution of
0442: \(f(z^p)=\mathscr R(z,f(z))\), with \(\mathscr R\) rational, belongs to
0443: \(\CC(z)\) \cite{Nishioka1985AlgebraicSolutions}.  Apply it with
0444: \(p=2\) and \(\mathscr R(z,Y)=Y^2/H(z)\).  Thus \(F\in\CC(z)\).
0445: Because the normalized Taylor germ of \(F\) has coefficients in \(\QQ\),
0446: coefficientwise Galois invariance gives \(F\in\QQ(z)\).  Taking
0447: \(R=F^{-1}\) in the displayed functional equation gives
0448: \[
0449:  H(z)=\frac{R(z^2)}{R(z)^2},\qquad R(0)=1.
0450: \]
0451: Normalized injectivity in \Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} proves
0452: uniqueness.  The rationality implication used here is Keiji Nishioka's theorem;
0453: the only descent specific to the present normalization is from the rational
0454: Taylor germ to \(\QQ(z)\).
0455: \end{proof}

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}
+
 The next estimate is not needed to reprove the special-value theorem below;
 it records an effective feature of the critical quadratic equation itself.
 The general zero-order theorem of T\"opfer requires the strict degree condition

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}

+\begin{theorem}[General rational critical \(p\)-Mahler lifting]
+\label{thm:general-rational-p-mahler-lifting}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=1\), and suppose

+\end{equation}

+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}
+ F_{H,p}(z)^p=H(z)F_{H,p}(z^p).

+ H(z)=\frac{R(z^p)}{R(z)^p}.
+\end{equation}

+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-positive-equivalence}
+ \prod_{\nu\ge0}H(\alpha^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu}}=1

+\end{equation}
+\end{theorem}

+\begin{proof}
+The logarithmic series in \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-product}
+converges normally on compact subdisks because
+\(\Log_0H(z)=O(z)\).  It defines a non-vanishing analytic function, and
+shifting the series proves \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}.
+
+Write \(H=P_0/P_1\) in reduced form with

+their coefficients.  If

+\Cref{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators} gives the exact estimate
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-denominator-input}
+ (pq)^{2h-1}f_h\in\ZZ,\qquad
+ \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq),
+\end{equation}
+where \(d_h\) is a common denominator for \(f_0,\ldots,f_h\).  Choose
+\(s\) with \(\abs\alpha<s<\min\{r,1\}\).  Cauchy's estimate gives
+\[
+ \abs{f_h}\le

+\]

+also bounds the logarithmic height of \(f_h\) linearly in \(h\).
+
+We may now apply Kumiko Nishioka's printed special-value theorem
+\cite[Theorem, p.~387]{Nishioka1982MahlerFunctionValues}.  For completeness,
+we check its parameters and orbit hypotheses.  In that theorem take
+\[

+\]

+exactly the bounds just proved, and the required strict inequality is
+\[
+ M(p+N)n^2=p^2<p^{2+1/L}=p^3.
+\]

+\(g(T^i\alpha)=P_0(\alpha^{p^i})\ne0\) for every \(i\), because
+\(\abs{\alpha^{p^i}}\le\abs\alpha<r\) and \(H\) is zero-free there.
+The product is analytic at every point of this orbit.  Thus the cited theorem
+implies that a transcendental \(F_{H,p}\) has transcendental value at
+\(\alpha\).  The assumed algebraicity of \(F_{H,p}(\alpha)\) therefore makes
+\(F_{H,p}\) algebraic over \(\CC(z)\).
+
+\Cref{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary} now gives the unique normalized
+rational function \(R=F_{H,p}^{-1}\) and

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}
+

 it records an effective feature of the critical quadratic equation itself.

+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}

+\begin{theorem}[General rational critical \(p\)-Mahler lifting]
+\label{thm:general-rational-p-mahler-lifting}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=1\), and suppose

+the normalized analytic function
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-product}
+ F_{H,p}(z):=\prod_{\nu\ge0}
+ H(z^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu-1}},
+ \qquad F_{H,p}(0)=1,
+\end{equation}
+using the logarithm germ at zero.  Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}
+ F_{H,p}(z)^p=H(z)F_{H,p}(z^p).
+\end{equation}
+If \(\alpha\ne0\) is algebraic,
+\[
+ \abs\alpha<\min\{r,1\},
+\]

+\(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\), normalized by \(R(0)=1\), such that
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-lifted-certificate}
+ H(z)=\frac{R(z^p)}{R(z)^p}.
+\end{equation}
+If, in addition, \(0<\alpha<r\) and \(H(t)>0\) on \([0,\alpha]\), then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-positive-equivalence}
+ \prod_{\nu\ge0}H(\alpha^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu}}=1
+ \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R(\alpha)=1.
+\end{equation}
+\end{theorem}

+\begin{proof}

+converges normally on compact subdisks because
+\(\Log_0H(z)=O(z)\).  It defines a non-vanishing analytic function, and
+shifting the series proves \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}.

+\begin{theorem}[General rational critical \(p\)-Mahler lifting]
+\label{thm:general-rational-p-mahler-lifting}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=1\), and suppose

+ H(z^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu-1}},
+ \qquad F_{H,p}(0)=1,
+\end{equation}

+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}

+\[

+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-lifted-certificate}
+ H(z)=\frac{R(z^p)}{R(z)^p}.
+\end{equation}

+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-positive-equivalence}
+ \prod_{\nu\ge0}H(\alpha^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu}}=1
+ \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R(\alpha)=1.
+\end{equation}
+\end{theorem}

+\begin{proof}

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}
+

 it records an effective feature of the critical quadratic equation itself.

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}
+

 it records an effective feature of the critical quadratic equation itself.

+\begin{theorem}[General rational critical \(p\)-Mahler lifting]
+\label{thm:general-rational-p-mahler-lifting}

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}
+

+\begin{theorem}[General rational critical \(p\)-Mahler lifting]
+\label{thm:general-rational-p-mahler-lifting}

+\end{equation}

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}
+

+\begin{theorem}[General rational critical \(p\)-Mahler lifting]
+\label{thm:general-rational-p-mahler-lifting}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=1\), and suppose

+the normalized analytic function

+ F_{H,p}(z):=\prod_{\nu\ge0}
+ H(z^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu-1}},
+ \qquad F_{H,p}(0)=1,
+\end{equation}
+using the logarithm germ at zero.  Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}
+ F_{H,p}(z)^p=H(z)F_{H,p}(z^p).
+\end{equation}

+\[
+ \abs\alpha<\min\{r,1\},

+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-lifted-certificate}
+ H(z)=\frac{R(z^p)}{R(z)^p}.
+\end{equation}
+If, in addition, \(0<\alpha<r\) and \(H(t)>0\) on \([0,\alpha]\), then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-positive-equivalence}
+ \prod_{\nu\ge0}H(\alpha^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu}}=1

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}
+

+\begin{theorem}[General rational critical \(p\)-Mahler lifting]
+\label{thm:general-rational-p-mahler-lifting}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=1\), and suppose

+the normalized analytic function

+ F_{H,p}(z):=\prod_{\nu\ge0}
+ H(z^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu-1}},
+ \qquad F_{H,p}(0)=1,
+\end{equation}
+using the logarithm germ at zero.  Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}
+ F_{H,p}(z)^p=H(z)F_{H,p}(z^p).
+\end{equation}

+\[
+ \abs\alpha<\min\{r,1\},
+\]

+\(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\), normalized by \(R(0)=1\), such that
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-lifted-certificate}
+ H(z)=\frac{R(z^p)}{R(z)^p}.
+\end{equation}
+If, in addition, \(0<\alpha<r\) and \(H(t)>0\) on \([0,\alpha]\), then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-positive-equivalence}
+ \prod_{\nu\ge0}H(\alpha^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu}}=1
+ \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R(\alpha)=1.
+\end{equation}
+\end{theorem}

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}

+\begin{theorem}[General rational critical \(p\)-Mahler lifting]
+\label{thm:general-rational-p-mahler-lifting}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=1\), and suppose
+that \(H\) has neither a zero nor a pole on \(\abs z<r\).  On that disk define
+the normalized analytic function
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-product}
+ F_{H,p}(z):=\prod_{\nu\ge0}
+ H(z^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu-1}},
+ \qquad F_{H,p}(0)=1,
+\end{equation}
+using the logarithm germ at zero.  Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}
+ F_{H,p}(z)^p=H(z)F_{H,p}(z^p).
+\end{equation}
+If \(\alpha\ne0\) is algebraic,
+\[
+ \abs\alpha<\min\{r,1\},
+\]
+and \(F_{H,p}(\alpha)\) is algebraic, then there is a unique
+\(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\), normalized by \(R(0)=1\), such that
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-lifted-certificate}
+ H(z)=\frac{R(z^p)}{R(z)^p}.
+\end{equation}
+If, in addition, \(0<\alpha<r\) and \(H(t)>0\) on \([0,\alpha]\), then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-positive-equivalence}
+ \prod_{\nu\ge0}H(\alpha^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu}}=1
+ \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R(\alpha)=1.
+\end{equation}
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The logarithmic series in \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-product}
+converges normally on compact subdisks because
+\(\Log_0H(z)=O(z)\).  It defines a non-vanishing analytic function, and
+shifting the series proves \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}.
+
+Write \(H=P_0/P_1\) in reduced form with
+\(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) and \(P_0(0)=P_1(0)=1\), and choose \(q\ge1\) clearing
+their coefficients.  If
+\(F_{H,p}(z)=\sum_{h\ge0}f_hz^h\), then
+\Cref{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators} gives the exact estimate
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-denominator-input}
+ (pq)^{2h-1}f_h\in\ZZ,\qquad
+ \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq),
+\end{equation}
+where \(d_h\) is a common denominator for \(f_0,\ldots,f_h\).  Choose
+\(s\) with \(\abs\alpha<s<\min\{r,1\}\).  Cauchy's estimate gives
+\[
+ \abs{f_h}\le
+ \max_{\abs z=s}\abs{F_{H,p}(z)}\,s^{-h}.
+\]
+Together with \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-denominator-input}, this
+also bounds the logarithmic height of \(f_h\) linearly in \(h\).
+
+We may now apply Kumiko Nishioka's printed special-value theorem
+\cite[Theorem, p.~387]{Nishioka1982MahlerFunctionValues}.  For completeness,
+we check its parameters and orbit hypotheses.  In that theorem take
+\[
+ Tz=z^p,\qquad
+ Q_0(z,u)=P_0(z),\qquad Q_1(z,u)=-P_1(z)u^p.
+\]
+The two \(Q_i\) are relatively prime in
+\(\overline{\QQ}[z,u]\), and its auxiliary polynomial may be chosen as

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}
+

 it records an effective feature of the critical quadratic equation itself.

+\begin{theorem}[General rational critical \(p\)-Mahler lifting]
+\label{thm:general-rational-p-mahler-lifting}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=1\), and suppose
+that \(H\) has neither a zero nor a pole on \(\abs z<r\).  On that disk define
+the normalized analytic function
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-product}
+ F_{H,p}(z):=\prod_{\nu\ge0}
+ H(z^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu-1}},
+ \qquad F_{H,p}(0)=1,
+\end{equation}
+using the logarithm germ at zero.  Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}
+ F_{H,p}(z)^p=H(z)F_{H,p}(z^p).
+\end{equation}
+If \(\alpha\ne0\) is algebraic,
+\[
+ \abs\alpha<\min\{r,1\},
+\]
+and \(F_{H,p}(\alpha)\) is algebraic, then there is a unique
+\(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\), normalized by \(R(0)=1\), such that
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-lifted-certificate}
+ H(z)=\frac{R(z^p)}{R(z)^p}.
+\end{equation}
+If, in addition, \(0<\alpha<r\) and \(H(t)>0\) on \([0,\alpha]\), then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-positive-equivalence}
+ \prod_{\nu\ge0}H(\alpha^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu}}=1
+ \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R(\alpha)=1.
+\end{equation}
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The logarithmic series in \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-product}
+converges normally on compact subdisks because
+\(\Log_0H(z)=O(z)\).  It defines a non-vanishing analytic function, and
+shifting the series proves \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}.
+
+Write \(H=P_0/P_1\) in reduced form with
+\(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) and \(P_0(0)=P_1(0)=1\), and choose \(q\ge1\) clearing
+their coefficients.  If
+\(F_{H,p}(z)=\sum_{h\ge0}f_hz^h\), then
+\Cref{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators} gives the exact estimate
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-denominator-input}
+ (pq)^{2h-1}f_h\in\ZZ,\qquad
+ \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq),
+\end{equation}
+where \(d_h\) is a common denominator for \(f_0,\ldots,f_h\).  Choose
+\(s\) with \(\abs\alpha<s<\min\{r,1\}\).  Cauchy's estimate gives
+\[
+ \abs{f_h}\le
+ \max_{\abs z=s}\abs{F_{H,p}(z)}\,s^{-h}.
+\]
+Together with \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-denominator-input}, this
+also bounds the logarithmic height of \(f_h\) linearly in \(h\).
+
+We may now apply Kumiko Nishioka's printed special-value theorem
+\cite[Theorem, p.~387]{Nishioka1982MahlerFunctionValues}.  For completeness,
+we check its parameters and orbit hypotheses.  In that theorem take
+\[
+ Tz=z^p,\qquad
+ Q_0(z,u)=P_0(z),\qquad Q_1(z,u)=-P_1(z)u^p.
+\]
+The two \(Q_i\) are relatively prime in
+\(\overline{\QQ}[z,u]\), and its auxiliary polynomial may be chosen as
+\(g(z)=P_0(z)\).  The numerical parameters are
+\[
+ N=0,\qquad n=1,\qquad m=p,\qquad M=p,\qquad U=1,\qquad L=1.
+\]
+The coefficient-size and common-denominator hypotheses with \(L=1\) are
+exactly the bounds just proved, and the required strict inequality is
+\[
+ M(p+N)n^2=p^2<p^{2+1/L}=p^3.
 \]
-Normalized injectivity in \Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} proves
-uniqueness.  The rationality implication used here is Keiji Nishioka's theorem;
-the only descent specific to the present normalization is from the rational
-Taylor germ to \(\QQ(z)\).
+Moreover \(T^i\alpha=\alpha^{p^i}\ne0\), and
+\(g(T^i\alpha)=P_0(\alpha^{p^i})\ne0\) for every \(i\), because
+\(\abs{\alpha^{p^i}}\le\abs\alpha<r\) and \(H\) is zero-free there.
+The product is analytic at every point of this orbit.  Thus the cited theorem
+implies that a transcendental \(F_{H,p}\) has transcendental value at
+\(\alpha\).  The assumed algebraicity of \(F_{H,p}(\alpha)\) therefore makes
+\(F_{H,p}\) algebraic over \(\CC(z)\).
+
+\Cref{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary} now gives the unique normalized
+rational function \(R=F_{H,p}^{-1}\) and
+\eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-lifted-certificate}.  Under the final
+positivity assumptions, the branch in
+\eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-product} is positive on
+\([0,\alpha]\), so \(R(\alpha)>0\), and
+\[
+ \prod_{\nu\ge0}H(\alpha^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu}}
+ =F_{H,p}(\alpha)^p=R(\alpha)^{-p}.
+\]
+This proves \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-positive-equivalence}.
 \end{proof}

+\begin{lemma}[Linear-exponent denominators for rational critical products]
+\label{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) have constant term one, and let
+\(q\ge1\) be an integer for which \(qP_0,qP_1\in\ZZ[z]\).  The unique formal
+series \(F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}f_nz^n\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-equation}
+ P_1(z)F(z)^p=P_0(z)F(z^p)
+\end{equation}
+obeys
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+ (pq)^{2n-1}f_n\in\ZZ\qquad(n\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+Consequently the first \(h+1\) coefficients have a common positive
+denominator \(d_h\) satisfying
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-common-denominator}
+ d_h\mid(pq)^{2h-1},
+ \qquad \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq)\qquad(h\ge1).
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(\widetilde P_i=qP_i\), so that
+\(\widetilde P_i\in\ZZ[z]\) and \(\widetilde P_i(0)=q\).  Comparison of the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in
+\(\widetilde P_1F^p=\widetilde P_0F(z^p)\) gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion}
+ pqf_n=\Phi_n(f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1}),
+\end{equation}
+where \(\Phi_n\) has integral coefficients.  Indeed, the only occurrence of
+\(f_n\) is obtained by choosing it in one of the \(p\) factors of \(F^p\)
+and constant terms everywhere else.  Every remaining linear term is \(f_j\)
+with \(j<n\); every remaining nonlinear monomial can be written
+\(f_{j_1}\cdots f_{j_s}\), where \(s\ge2\), all \(j_i\ge1\), and
+\(j_1+\cdots+j_s\le n\).
+
+Set \(c=pq\).  We prove \eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-denominator-bound}
+by induction.  If it holds below \(n\), a linear term \(f_j\), \(j<n\), has
+denominator dividing \(c^{2j-1}\), hence \(c^{2n-2}\).  A nonlinear monomial
+as above has denominator dividing
+\[
+ c^{\sum_i(2j_i-1)}
+ =c^{2\sum_i j_i-s}\mid c^{2n-2}.
+\]
+Thus \(c^{2n-2}\Phi_n\in\ZZ\), and division by \(c\) in
+\eqref{eq:rational-critical-mahler-recursion} proves the induction step.
+The exponents are increasing with \(n\), so the common-denominator assertion
+and its logarithmic bound follow immediately.
+\end{proof}
+

 it records an effective feature of the critical quadratic equation itself.

+\begin{theorem}[General rational critical \(p\)-Mahler lifting]
+\label{thm:general-rational-p-mahler-lifting}
+Let \(p\ge2\), let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=1\), and suppose
+that \(H\) has neither a zero nor a pole on \(\abs z<r\).  On that disk define
+the normalized analytic function
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-product}
+ F_{H,p}(z):=\prod_{\nu\ge0}
+ H(z^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu-1}},
+ \qquad F_{H,p}(0)=1,
+\end{equation}
+using the logarithm germ at zero.  Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}
+ F_{H,p}(z)^p=H(z)F_{H,p}(z^p).
+\end{equation}
+If \(\alpha\ne0\) is algebraic,
+\[
+ \abs\alpha<\min\{r,1\},
+\]
+and \(F_{H,p}(\alpha)\) is algebraic, then there is a unique
+\(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\), normalized by \(R(0)=1\), such that
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-lifted-certificate}
+ H(z)=\frac{R(z^p)}{R(z)^p}.
+\end{equation}
+If, in addition, \(0<\alpha<r\) and \(H(t)>0\) on \([0,\alpha]\), then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-positive-equivalence}
+ \prod_{\nu\ge0}H(\alpha^{p^\nu})^{p^{-\nu}}=1
+ \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R(\alpha)=1.
+\end{equation}
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The logarithmic series in \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-product}
+converges normally on compact subdisks because
+\(\Log_0H(z)=O(z)\).  It defines a non-vanishing analytic function, and
+shifting the series proves \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-equation}.
+
+Write \(H=P_0/P_1\) in reduced form with
+\(P_0,P_1\in\QQ[z]\) and \(P_0(0)=P_1(0)=1\), and choose \(q\ge1\) clearing
+their coefficients.  If
+\(F_{H,p}(z)=\sum_{h\ge0}f_hz^h\), then
+\Cref{lem:rational-critical-mahler-denominators} gives the exact estimate
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-denominator-input}
+ (pq)^{2h-1}f_h\in\ZZ,\qquad
+ \log d_h\le(2h-1)\log(pq),
+\end{equation}
+where \(d_h\) is a common denominator for \(f_0,\ldots,f_h\).  Choose
+\(s\) with \(\abs\alpha<s<\min\{r,1\}\).  Cauchy's estimate gives
+\[
+ \abs{f_h}\le
+ \max_{\abs z=s}\abs{F_{H,p}(z)}\,s^{-h}.
+\]
+Together with \eqref{eq:general-critical-p-mahler-denominator-input}, this
+also bounds the logarithmic height of \(f_h\) linearly in \(h\).
+
+We may now apply Kumiko Nishioka's printed special-value theorem
+\cite[Theorem, p.~387]{Nishioka1982MahlerFunctionValues}.  For completeness,
+we check its parameters and orbit hypotheses.  In that theorem take
+\[
+ Tz=z^p,\qquad
+ Q_0(z,u)=P_0(z),\qquad Q_1(z,u)=-P_1(z)u^p.
+\]
+The two \(Q_i\) are relatively prime in
+\(\overline{\QQ}[z,u]\), and its auxiliary polynomial may be chosen as
+\(g(z)=P_0(z)\).  The numerical parameters are
+\[

+\]
+The coefficient-size and common-denominator hypotheses with \(L=1\) are

+\[

 \]
